questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Mean, median, mode and range
questions.stem: On seven evenings a café had $6$, $9$, $6$, $11$, $15$, $6$ and $12$ tables occupied at eight o'clock. Find the mode.
questions.solution:
The mode is the value that occurs most often. It is read off from the counts, not from the size of the values.

Tally the seven readings:
$$6 \text{ occurs } 3 \text{ times},\quad 9,\ 11,\ 12,\ 15 \text{ occur once each}.$$

No other value reaches three, so the mode is $6$.
distractorRationale: Correct. $6$ appears three times and every other value appears once.
This is the median: the middle value once the list is sorted, which is not the same as the most frequent value.
This is the fourth entry of the list as it is written down. The middle of an unsorted list carries no meaning.
This is the largest value. The mode is the most common value, not the biggest one.

verification.expression: [6, 9, 11, 12, 15].reduce(function (best, v) { return [6,9,6,11,15,6,12].filter(function (w) { return w === v; }).length > [6,9,6,11,15,6,12].filter(function (w) { return w === best; }).length ? v : best; })

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Mean, median, mode and range
questions.stem: Over one week a kiosk sold $14$, $9$, $22$, $9$, $17$, $30$ and $12$ newspapers on its seven days. Find the range.
questions.solution:
The range measures spread. It is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The largest sale is $30$ and the smallest is $9$, so
$$\text{range} = 30 - 9 = 21.$$

The range is a single number, not a pair of numbers.
distractorRationale: This is the smallest value, which is also the mode. The range is a difference, not one of the readings.
This is the largest value on its own; the smallest was never subtracted.
Added the two extreme values instead of subtracting them.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Mean, median, mode and range
questions.stem: Six parcels have masses, in kilograms, of $15$, $4$, $11$, $16$, $6$ and $14$. Find the median mass.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — sort the masses.**
$$4,\ 6,\ 11,\ 14,\ 15,\ 16.$$

**Step 2 — locate the middle.** There are $6$ values, an even count, so no single value sits in the middle. The two central values are the third and the fourth, namely $11$ and $14$.

**Step 3 — average them.**
$$\text{median} = \frac{11 + 14}{2} = 12.5.$$
distractorRationale: Took the lower of the two central values on its own. It is also the mean, $\dfrac{66}{6}$, which for this data happens to coincide with it.
This is the range, $16 - 4$, a measure of spread rather than of centre.
Correct. With an even count the median is the mean of the two central values, $\dfrac{11 + 14}{2} = 12.5$.
Took the upper of the two central values on its own, instead of averaging the pair.

verification.expression: [15, 4, 11, 16, 6, 14].slice().sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; }).slice(2, 4).reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0) / 2

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Mean, median, mode and range
questions.stem: Six scores have a mean of $12$. A seventh score is included and the mean of all seven rises to $13$. Find the seventh score.
questions.solution:
A mean is a total divided by a count, so turn each mean back into a total.

**Step 1 — the total before.**
$$6 \times 12 = 72.$$

**Step 2 — the total after.** There are now seven scores:
$$7 \times 13 = 91.$$

**Step 3 — the difference is the new score.**
$$91 - 72 = 19.$$

A check: the new score has to sit above $13$ to pull the mean upwards, and $19$ does.
distractorRationale: Used $6 \times 13 - 6 \times 12$, keeping the count at six after the extra score was added.
Used $7 \times 13 - 7 \times 12$, applying the new count of seven to the old total as well.
Restated the new mean. A single value equal to the mean would leave the mean unchanged, not raise it.
Correct. $7 \times 13 - 6 \times 12 = 91 - 72 = 19$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Variance and standard deviation
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the mean.**
$$\bar{x} = \frac{4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12}{5} = \frac{40}{5} = 8.$$

**Step 2 — the deviations and their squares.**
$$-4,\ -2,\ 0,\ 2,\ 4 \quad\longrightarrow\quad 16,\ 4,\ 0,\ 4,\ 16.$$

**Step 3 — average the squares.** The squared deviations total $40$, and there are $5$ values:
$$s^{2} = \frac{40}{5} = 8.$$
distractorRationale: This is $\sqrt{8}$, the standard deviation. The question asks for the variance, which is the square of it.
Correct. The squared deviations total $40$, and $\dfrac{40}{5} = 8$.
Divided by $4$ instead of by $5$. The divisor is the number of values, not one fewer.
Left the total of the squared deviations undivided.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Variance and standard deviation
questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of $3$, $5$, $6$, $7$ and $9$.
distractorRationale: Correct. The variance is $\dfrac{20}{5} = 4$, and its square root is $2$.
Divided the total $20$ by $4$ rather than by $5$ before taking the root, so the divisor was one too small.
Stopped at the variance and never took the square root.
Left the total of the squared deviations undivided and unrooted.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Variance and standard deviation
questions.stem: The variance of $x_{1},\ x_{2},\ \ldots,\ x_{8}$ is $3$. Find the variance of $2x_{1}+5,\ 2x_{2}+5,\ \ldots,\ 2x_{8}+5$.
questions.solution:
Variance measures spread about the mean, so treat the two parts of the transformation separately.

**The $+5$.** Adding $5$ to every value slides the whole data set along, and the mean slides with it. Each deviation from the mean is unchanged, so the variance is unchanged.

**The $\times 2$.** Doubling every value doubles every deviation. Variance uses *squared* deviations, so it is multiplied by $2^{2} = 4$.

In general, for $y = ax + b$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(y) = a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(x) = 2^{2} \times 3 = 12.$$
distractorRationale: Assumed the transformation leaves the variance alone. That is true of the $+5$, but not of the $\times 2$.
Multiplied by the scale factor $2$ instead of by its square $2^{2}$.
Applied the whole transformation to the variance itself, computing $2 \times 3 + 5$. The shift $+5$ must not be carried across.
Correct. $\operatorname{Var}(2x + 5) = 2^{2} \times 3 = 12$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / Variance and standard deviation
questions.stem: The mean of six measurements is $5$, and the sum of their squares is $174$. Find the variance of the six measurements.
questions.solution:
The individual measurements are not given, so use the form of the variance that needs only totals:
$$s^{2} = \overline{x^{2}} - \bar{x}^{2},$$
the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

**Step 1 — the mean of the squares.**
$$\overline{x^{2}} = \frac{174}{6} = 29.$$

**Step 2 — the square of the mean.**
$$\bar{x}^{2} = 5^{2} = 25.$$

**Step 3 — subtract.**
$$s^{2} = 29 - 25 = 4.$$
distractorRationale: This is $\sqrt{4}$, the standard deviation, not the variance.
Subtracted the mean itself rather than the square of the mean, computing $29 - 5$.
Stopped at $\dfrac{174}{6}$, the mean of the squares, with the $\bar{x}^{2}$ term never subtracted.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The binomial distribution
questions.stem: Each seed of one variety germinates with probability $0.2$, independently of the others. Four seeds are sown. Find the probability that exactly one germinates.
questions.solution:
The four seeds are independent and each has the same germination probability, so the number that germinate is binomial with $n = 4$ and $p = 0.2$.

**Step 1 — one particular arrangement.** One seed germinates and the other three do not:
$$0.2 \times 0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.8 = 0.2 \times 0.8^{3} = 0.1024.$$

**Step 2 — count the arrangements.** The germinating seed can be any one of the four, so there are $\binom{4}{1} = 4$ arrangements, each with the same probability.

**Step 3 — multiply.**
$$4 \times 0.1024 = 0.4096.$$
distractorRationale: This is one arrangement only: the factor $\binom{4}{1} = 4$ was left out.
Restated $p$, the germination probability for a single seed.
Correct. $\binom{4}{1} \times 0.2 \times 0.8^{3} = 4 \times 0.1024 = 0.4096$.
This is $1 - 0.8^{4}$, the probability that *at least* one germinates, which also allows two, three or four.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The binomial distribution
questions.stem: A machine seals a carton incorrectly with probability $0.3$, independently of the other cartons. Ten cartons are checked. The probability that exactly two of them are sealed incorrectly is
questions.solution:
The count of badly sealed cartons is binomial with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.3$, so
$$P(X = k) = \binom{10}{k} \, 0.3^{k} \, 0.7^{\,10-k}.$$

**Step 1 — the exponents.** Exactly two cartons are sealed incorrectly, so $0.3$ carries the exponent $2$ and the remaining $10 - 2 = 8$ good cartons give $0.7^{8}$.

**Step 2 — the coefficient.** The two faulty cartons can be any two of the ten:
$$\binom{10}{2} = \frac{10 \times 9}{2 \times 1} = 45.$$

**Step 3 — put it together.**
$$P(X = 2) = 45 \times 0.3^{2} \times 0.7^{8}.$$
distractorRationale: The exponents are right but the coefficient $\binom{10}{2}$ is missing, so only one arrangement of the two faulty cartons is counted.
Used $10$ in place of $\binom{10}{2} = 45$. That coefficient would suit exactly *one* faulty carton, not two.
Correct. $\binom{10}{2} = 45$, and the exponents $2$ and $8$ match the two faulty and eight sound cartons.
The exponents are swapped: $0.3$ describes a faulty carton, so it must carry the exponent $2$, not $8$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The binomial distribution
questions.stem: A component passes a test with probability $0.6$, independently of the others. One hundred components are tested, and $X$ is the number that pass. Find the variance of $X$.
questions.solution:
$X$ counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials that all share the same success probability, so $X$ is binomial with $n = 100$ and $p = 0.6$.

For a binomial variable,
$$E(X) = np, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1-p).$$

Substituting $n = 100$ and $p = 0.6$:
$$\operatorname{Var}(X) = 100 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 = 24.$$
distractorRationale: This is $\sqrt{24}$, the standard deviation of $X$. The variance is its square.
Correct. $np(1-p) = 100 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 = 24$.
Computed $n(1-p) = 100 \times 0.4$, the expected number of components that fail.
Computed $np = 100 \times 0.6$, the mean of $X$ rather than its variance.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The normal distribution
questions.stem: A variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $60$, so its curve is symmetric about $60$. Given $P(X > 72) = 0.15$, find $P(X < 48)$.
questions.solution:
Compare the two boundaries with the mean:
$$72 - 60 = 12, \qquad 60 - 48 = 12.$$
The two values sit the same distance from the mean, one above and one below.

The curve is symmetric about $60$, so the tail to the left of $48$ is a mirror image of the tail to the right of $72$. Mirror images have equal area:
$$P(X < 48) = P(X > 72) = 0.15.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. $48$ and $72$ are both $12$ from the mean, so the two outer tails have equal area.
This is $0.5 - 0.15$, the area between the mean and $72$, not the tail beyond $48$.
This is $1 - 2 \times 0.15$, the area between $48$ and $72$ — the middle, not a tail.
This is $1 - 0.15 = P(X < 72)$, which includes the whole left half of the curve as well as the tail asked for.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The normal distribution
questions.stem: The masses of a batch of bricks are normally distributed with mean $2.4$ and standard deviation $0.2$, in kilograms. For a normal distribution, $95.44\%$ of the values lie within two standard deviations of the mean. Find the proportion of bricks with mass below $2.8$ kilograms.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — measure $2.8$ in standard deviations.**
$$2.8 = 2.4 + 2 \times 0.2,$$
so $2.8$ sits exactly two standard deviations above the mean.

**Step 2 — split the given band.** The stated $0.9544$ covers the band from $2.0$ to $2.8$, which straddles the mean. By symmetry, half of it lies above the mean:
$$P(2.4 < X < 2.8) = \frac{0.9544}{2} = 0.4772.$$

**Step 3 — add the lower half of the curve.** Everything below the mean also counts:
$$P(X < 2.8) = 0.5 + 0.4772 = 0.9772.$$
distractorRationale: This is $\dfrac{1 - 0.9544}{2}$, the upper tail — the proportion *above* $2.8$, not below it.
This is half the given band, $P(2.4 < X < 2.8)$, with the lower half of the curve left out.
This is the stated band itself, $P(2.0 < X < 2.8)$, which wrongly excludes every brick lighter than $2.0$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The normal distribution
questions.stem: The lifetime $X$ of a lamp, in hours, is normally distributed with mean $900$, and $P(880 < X < 920) = 0.68$. Two lamps are picked independently. Find the probability that both last longer than $920$ hours.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the area outside the band.** The band from $880$ to $920$ holds $0.68$, so the two tails together hold
$$1 - 0.68 = 0.32.$$

**Step 2 — split the tails.** The band is centred on the mean $900$, since $900 - 880 = 920 - 900 = 20$. So the two tails are mirror images and share the $0.32$ equally:
$$P(X > 920) = \frac{0.32}{2} = 0.16.$$

**Step 3 — two lamps.** The lamps are independent, so multiply:
$$0.16 \times 0.16 = 0.0256.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. Each lamp exceeds $920$ hours with probability $0.16$, and $0.16^{2} = 0.0256$.
Squared $0.32$, the two tails together, instead of squaring the single upper tail $0.16$.
This is the probability for one lamp only; the second lamp was never brought in.
This is $1 - 0.68$, the chance that one lamp falls outside the band — either tail, and for one lamp only.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-4 / Probability and Statistics / Statistics and Distributions / The normal distribution
questions.stem: Marks in a test are normally distributed with mean $70$ and standard deviation $8$. For a normal distribution, $68.26\%$ of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and $95.44\%$ within two. Of $2000$ candidates, estimate how many scored between $62$ and $86$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — put the two boundaries in standard deviations.**
$$62 = 70 - 8 \quad (\text{one below}), \qquad 86 = 70 + 2 \times 8 \quad (\text{two above}).$$
The interval is lopsided, so the two given percentages cannot be used directly. Split it at the mean.

**Step 2 — the part below the mean.** Half of the one-standard-deviation band:
$$P(62 < X < 70) = \frac{0.6826}{2} = 0.3413.$$

**Step 3 — the part above the mean.** Half of the two-standard-deviation band:
$$P(70 < X < 86) = \frac{0.9544}{2} = 0.4772.$$

**Step 4 — add, then scale to the group.**
$$0.3413 + 0.4772 = 0.8185, \qquad 2000 \times 0.8185 = 1637.$$
distractorRationale: Used $0.4772$ alone, the part from $70$ to $86$, leaving out everything between $62$ and the mean.
Used the full one-standard-deviation band $0.6826$, which covers $62$ to $78$ — the upper boundary is wrong.
Used the full two-standard-deviation band $0.9544$, which covers $54$ to $86$ — the lower boundary is wrong.
